answers.explanation: 4xx errors are the client's fault, so the same request will fail again. A 5xx means the server failed, and a retry might work. 429 Too Many Requests is the exception that says to slow down and try later.
DELETE changes state, so it isn't safe, but deleting twice has the same effect as deleting once. GET is safe and idempotent, while POST and PATCH aren't necessarily idempotent.
Idempotency is about the effect, not the response. Either way book 8 ends up deleted. That's what makes it safe to retry a timed-out DELETE without knowing whether the first one ran.

The client generates one key per logical operation. The server remembers the response for each key it has succeeded with, and returns it again for a retry. Checking the list first races with the original request, which may still be in flight.

With offsets, the database still walks past every earlier row, and an insert at the top shifts every page, so items repeat or get skipped. A cursor names the last item seen, so the next page is always "items after this one."

Needing extra round trips for related data is under-fetching. Receiving fields you don't need is over-fetching. GraphQL avoids both by letting the client name exactly the fields it wants, in one request.
A .proto file assigns each field a number (title = 2), and the encoding sends that number and a compact binary value instead of repeating "title" as text in every message.

A local call either runs or throws, in nanoseconds. A remote one crosses the network: it can be lost, delayed, or run without the reply arriving. Code has to handle timeouts, retries, and idempotency explicitly.
One query for the list plus one per book is the N+1 problem. Collecting the 50 author ids and loading them in a single query (what DataLoader automates) makes it two queries in total.
HTTP caches and CDNs key on the method and URL, and only cache safe GETs. With GraphQL, every query is a POST to one endpoint, so you need your own caching layer.
